briefing:
SITUATION BRIEFING — Round 6

It is Day 2, 18:00 CET. Ultimatum expires in 14 hours. POSSIBLE NUCLEAR WARHEAD LOADING DETECTED.

MILITARY: Ford CSG has entered the Baltic Sea. SEAD target package finalized: 47 targets, 200+ planned sorties. All NATO ground forces at final assembly positions. Russian forces in deep defense, supply declining.

NUCLEAR ALERT: At 17:45, satellite imagery showed Iskander-M loading bay doors OPEN in Kaliningrad. Technicians in NBC gear visible. CANNOT determine if warheads are conventional or nuclear. Washington-Moscow hotline activated for first time.

DIPLOMATIC: Modi mediation failed — Putin says corridor 'non-negotiable.' China's peace framework shelved. Bundestag approved German operations 538-89. Turkey closed Straits + F-35/S-400 deal. Hungary's extension demand rejected by all allies.

FORCES READY:
- SEAD: F-35s (Lakenheath), EA-18G (Ford), Eurofighters, Rafales, Finnish MLRS
- Ground: Polish 18th Mech (south), German 45th (north), V Corps arty, UK 4th Bde en route
- Naval: Ford CSG in Baltic, Danish Straits closed, Swedish subs deployed
- Russian: 5 BTGs fortified, 2x S-400, Iskander-M (possibly loading), EW active, 3 subs in Norwegian Sea

ECONOMIC: Oil $108. Euro at $0.99. Markets in freefall.

CRITICAL: The Iskander loading activity is THE crisis within the crisis. If Russia is loading nuclear warheads, this changes everything. The Washington-Moscow hotline call will determine whether the world steps back from the nuclear brink or crosses it.
narrative:
As the NATO ultimatum clock counted down from 22 hours to 14, the world entered the strangest phase of the crisis — a period diplomats would later call 'the phoney peace,' when everyone knew war was coming but no one would be the first to fire.

The diplomatic track, demanded by both Washington and Budapest, produced precisely what the hawks had predicted: nothing. India's Prime Minister Modi called Putin at 10:30 CET, offering to carry a message to Washington. Putin's response was revealing: he was willing to discuss 'the framework of the humanitarian corridor' and 'mutual security guarantees,' but the corridor itself was 'non-negotiable.' When Modi relayed this to Rubio at 12:00, the US Secretary of State replied curtly: 'Russia's position makes military action inevitable. Thank the Prime Minister for his efforts.' China's Wang Yi made a similar attempt, tabling a 'Six-Point Peace Framework' at the UN that was so deliberately vague — 'respect all parties' security concerns' — that it satisfied no one and was quietly shelved.

The German Bundestag held its emergency session at 14:00. Chancellor Merz's speech was unexpectedly powerful: 'For decades, Germans said never again. We said it after 1945, we said it after reunification, we said it with Zeitenwende. Today, I tell you what never again means: never again will Germany stand by while a European democracy is occupied. German soldiers are in Lithuania. They did not volunteer for a peacetime garrison — they volunteered to defend freedom. The Bundestag must give them the authority to do so.' The vote passed 538-89, with only AfD and BSW opposing. The authorization covered defensive operations and SEAD support for 90 days.

At 15:00 CET — with 17 hours remaining on the ultimatum — Turkey made its move. Erdogan announced the formal closure of the Danish-Turkish Straits to all Russian military vessel transit, invoking the Montreux Convention. More significantly, Turkey confirmed its F-35 reinstatement deal: Ankara would transfer its S-400 systems to US custody at Incirlik within 90 days in exchange for 40 F-35As beginning delivery in 2027. The deal had been negotiated in the margins of the crisis. Turkey simultaneously offered Ankara as a venue for post-conflict negotiations — positioning itself as both warrior and peacemaker.

The Ford Carrier Strike Group entered the Baltic Sea at 16:30 CET, passing through the Danish Straits with a Danish Navy escort. The carrier's EA-18G Growler squadron — the most sophisticated electronic warfare aircraft in the world — would be critical for the SEAD campaign. Russian radar tracked the group's passage. In Kaliningrad, commanders reported to Moscow that the correlation of forces was shifting decisively against them.

Hungary made one final attempt to delay. Orbán called an emergency press conference at 17:00, announcing that he had received 'positive signals' from Moscow about negotiations and demanding a 48-hour extension of the ultimatum. The response from NATO capitals was uniform and brutal. Poland's Foreign Minister stated flatly: 'Hungary's suggestion is noted and rejected.' France and Germany issued a joint statement: 'The ultimatum stands.' Even Italy's Meloni, who had been sympathetic to diplomatic efforts, told Orbán privately: 'Viktor, the train has left the station. Get on it or get left behind.'

Behind the scenes, the military preparations were reaching their climax. SACEUR's operations center at SHAPE was running 24/7. The SEAD target package was finalized: 47 priority targets including S-400 batteries, Iskander-M positions, EW nodes, command posts, and radar installations. F-35s from RAF Lakenheath would strike from the north, Growlers from the Ford would jam from the sea, Polish and Finnish long-range fires would suppress from the south. The plan called for 200+ sorties in the first 12 hours.

And then, at 17:45 CET, satellite imagery detected something that sent a chill through every intelligence agency watching: the loading bay doors on the Iskander-M launchers in Kaliningrad were open. Technicians in NBC protective gear were visible near the launchers. It was impossible to determine from imagery alone whether the warheads being loaded were conventional or nuclear. The Presidential hotline between Washington and Moscow rang for the first time since the crisis began.

surprises: The Iskander loading activity was NOT authorized by Putin. As with the previous game, it was initiated by the Kaliningrad garrison commander, General-Lieutenant Frolov, who feared that the SEAD campaign would destroy his forces without any credible deterrent. When Putin learned of the loading via the hotline call with the US President, he was reportedly furious — not at the Americans for detecting it, but at Frolov for acting without authorization. The hotline call lasted 47 minutes. What was said remains classified, but within 90 minutes of the call ending, the loading activity ceased and the Iskander bay doors were closed. The world had come within hours of a rogue commander triggering nuclear war.
